name: Odori Park
label: Odori Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'さっぽろテレビ塔' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'さっぽろテレビ塔' (way/199758828): middle (48 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/64733385: large area 'Ōdōri Park' (1687 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Long green park through the city centre, home of the Snow Festival.

text.description: Odori Park is a long, green strip through the middle of Sapporo, running east to west for about 1.5 km and splitting the city into its northern and southern halves. It began as a firebreak in the 1870s, was later used as a street and then laid out as a walking area, and today it is a string of flower gardens and event grounds. The Sapporo Snow Festival and the Lilac Festival both take place here. It photographs well because the park is so straight and so long. From above, the whole ribbon of trees and gardens lines up against the city grid, with mountains behind. The classic view is from the observation deck of the Sapporo TV Tower, which was erected in 1957 and stands at the east end of the park. Looking west from the deck, you see the full length of the park, and on a clear day Ishikari Bay beyond. Dusk is the best moment, when the sunset and the first street lights can be shot together. If you would rather stay on the ground, a second option is to stand in the park and photograph the tower rising over the trees, with the subway exit sign bearing the city's name in the foreground. Another is the Sunken Garden, where roses in soft evening light look best, with the quieter western end of the park behind. What you see changes with the seasons, since winter festival structures and flower displays vary through the year.
text.geographic_location: Odori Park lies in the centre of Sapporo, in Hokkaido, running east to west between the northern and southern halves of the city. The Sapporo TV Tower stands at its eastern end, in the Nishi 1 chōme block.
text.directions_text: Ōdōri Station on the Sapporo Municipal Subway lies right at the park, and the TV Tower is at the east end, in the Nishi 1 chōme block. The middle of the park is about 835 m west of the tower. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole length of the park, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view of the city grid. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the mountains or one flower bed.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at さっぽろテレビ塔 (observation deck, looking west along the park; the tower sits at the east end of Odori Park). A bird's-eye view of the whole length of Odori Park, with the city grid, the surrounding mountains and, on clear days, Ishikari Bay beyond. Face west, along the length of the park. From here the photo shows a bird's-eye view of the whole park, with the city grid, the surrounding mountains and, on clear days, Ishikari Bay beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the park up with a vertical grid line so it runs straight away from you. Keep a little sky and the mountains in the top third. For a different picture, go down to the park and shoot the tower rising over the trees, framed by the subway exit sign bearing the city's name.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the park to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sunset sky keeps its colour. When the lights come on, try night mode and hold the phone as still as you can. Hold the lens close to the glass to cut reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk, when you can shoot the sunset and the first street lights together. Arrive a little early to get a good spot on the deck.

text.access_note: The Sapporo TV Tower observation deck is a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go for opening times, prices and the latest details; the park itself is a public space.
claims_not_in_sources: Holding a phone close to the glass of an observation deck helps reduce reflections.
Arriving early at the deck helps you get a good spot at dusk.
The park itself is open to walk through freely (public space).
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep sunset colours in a bright sky.

name: Sapporo Beer Museum
label: Sapporo Beer Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sapporo Beer Museum' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/219728956: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sapporo Beer Museum' (112 m across).
notes: Red brick former brewery with a museum and beer hall.

text.description: The Sapporo Beer Museum is a red-brick Meiji-era building in Sapporo Garden Park, and the outside is easy to enjoy even if you never go in. The brick walls, arched windows, red star emblems and the tall chimney behind the roofline give you plenty to work with. The building went up in 1890 as a factory for the Sapporo Sugar Company. The Sapporo Beer Company bought it in 1903 and turned it into a brewery. It opened as a museum in July 1987, and it is described as the only beer museum in Japan. It was registered as a Hokkaidō Heritage site in 2004. The Sapporo Beer Garden is in the south wing of the building. Start at the front entrance, where the facade and the red star give you the classic shot. Then walk round the building and try the side walls for a different angle. Keep your phone level so the vertical lines of the chimney and walls stay straight. If you plan to go inside, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Sapporo Garden Park in Higashi-ku, on the east side of Sapporo. The Sapporo Beer Garden is connected to the museum, and the Ario Sapporo shopping mall is also in the park.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Sapporo Garden Park in Higashi-ku, the nearest well-known area. Once in the park, look for the red-brick building with the tall chimney. The phone icon on the map is in the middle of the building outline on the map, so use it to orient yourself, then move to the front entrance for the main shot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the front facade and the red star. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want the whole building and chimney in one frame. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the star emblems and arched windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From the front the photo shows the red-brick facade with its red star emblems, arched windows and the tall brick chimney rising behind it. For a different angle, walk along the side walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the facade with the vertical lines so the walls do not lean. Put the red star in the upper third and let the chimney rise behind it. Then walk round the building and try the side walls for a more graphic shot of brick and windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick wall to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the red brick keeps its colour. When you use the ultra-wide lens close to the walls, stay square on to the building to limit distortion.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, which one guide recommends for exterior shots.

text.access_note: The outside of the building can be photographed from the park, but the museum itself is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

photo.artist: The original uploader was K. Takeda at Japanese Wikipedia.

name: Nijo Market
label: Nijo Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Nijo Market' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W64742255 (Nijo Market): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: Nijo Market is a row of seafood stalls in Sapporo, and the stall row is what makes it worth a phone photo. Along the L-shaped stretch of South 2nd Avenue (Minami 2-jo), crab, sea urchin, salmon roe and fish are laid out on display. Colourful signs and fish-shaped signboards hang around them, so almost every frame has colour and a clear subject. Walk the whole row rather than stopping at the first stall. That lets you take wide scenes of the street and then move in on the close-up displays. The roadside mascot statues are a popular photo stop too, and they work well as a foreground for a wider shot. Go in the morning, before about 10:00. If you want a quieter picture, a second option is Sōseigawa Park nearby. From the riverbank you can look back across the Sosei River toward the market buildings, with a calmer foreground. Stall hours vary from shop to shop, so check before making a special trip. Wider shots of the general atmosphere are usually fine, but ask permission before taking close-ups of the people working at the stalls.
text.geographic_location: Nijo Market is in Sapporo, along South 2nd Avenue (Minami 2-jo). The Sosei River and Sōseigawa Park are close by.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Head to South 2nd Avenue (Minami 2-jo) in Sapporo and walk the L-shaped stretch of the street to find the stall row. The phone icon on the map is at the market itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the stall displays and signs. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole street and the mascot statues, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of crab, urchin and roe without leaning over the stalls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on the stall row along the L-shaped stretch of South 2nd Avenue (Minami 2-jo).
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Take a wide shot first to show the whole row and its signs. Then move along and frame single displays close up. Use the gridlines to keep the stall fronts straight, and put a mascot statue in the foreground for scale. For a calmer alternative, try the view back across the Sosei River from Sōseigawa Park.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the display you want to focus on, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the bright signs wash out. Portrait mode can help with a single crab or a bowl of roe, if your phone allows it.

text.access_note: The stalls are along South 2nd Avenue, and hours vary from shop to shop, so check before making a special trip.

name: Susukino
label: Susukino
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'COCONO SUSUKINO' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'COCONO SUSUKINO' (way/378066770): middle (131 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q869175: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Neon nightlife district with the famous Nikka whisky sign.

text.description:
Susukino is a district of Sapporo known for entertainment and nightlife, full of restaurants, bars and hotels, and the photo to take here is at the crossing between Nishi 3 and Nishi 4 chome at Minami 4. Neon signs cover the buildings around it. The most famous is the Nikka sign on the front of the Susukino Building, which shows the Nikka symbol, the King of Blenders, against a background that keeps changing colour. Trams pass through the junction, which gives a street photo some movement.

The name is usually translated as 'zebra grass field'. The district dates from 1871, when the pioneering authority for Hokkaidō first laid it out, and it has changed a great deal since. Today it hosts a Susukino Festival each August and ice statues along the street every February, both of which can make a good backdrop if you happen to visit then.

The usual picture is taken from the crosswalk, which can be crowded. A calmer option is the 2nd-floor outdoor terrace of COCONO SUSUKINO. It faces the sign head-on across the intersection, with the crossing lights in the background. Reach it by the escalator at the building's corner, beside the Nikka statue. One travel guide says the Ferris wheel can also be seen from here. If the terrace is shut or busy, the crossing itself is the other good spot. Keep your phone strap round your wrist near the road.
text.geographic_location: Susukino is in Chūō-ku, Sapporo. The Nikka sign stands above the Susukino Crossing, at the junction of Nishi 3–4 chome and Minami 4.
text.directions_text: Head for the Susukino district in Chūō-ku, Sapporo, on foot or by local transport or taxi, and ask for the Susukino Crossing. Look for the COCONO SUSUKINO building at the corner with the Nikka statue, then take the escalator up to the 2nd-floor terrace. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the sign and the crossing lights together. If your phone has a telephoto (2x or more), use it to fill the frame with the sign and cut out the clutter below. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole junction and the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at COCONO SUSUKINO (2nd-floor outdoor terrace, reached by escalator from the building's corner next to the Nikka statue). A closer, head-on view of the Nikka sign across the intersection, with the Susukino crossing lights in the background. Reached by the escalator from the building's corner next to the Nikka statue. From the terrace you look head-on at the Nikka sign across the intersection, with the Susukino crossing lights behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the sign on one of the upper intersections, leaving the crossing lights and any passing tram in the lower part of the frame. Keep the phone level so the building edges stay straight. One guide suggests the Ferris wheel is also visible from here, so look around before you choose your framing. The crossing itself is the busier alternative, and is good for neon signs and trams.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sign to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright neon keeps its colour instead of turning white. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on the rail to keep the phone steady. A Live Photo can catch a tram passing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the neon and the sign are lit, or on a rainy evening when the road reflects the lights.

text.access_note: The crossing is an ordinary public street, but the terrace belongs to a shopping building, so check the official site before you go for access times.

name: Hokkaido Shrine
label: Hokkaido Shrine
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hokkaido Shrine No.1 Torii Gate' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/146432491: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hokkaido Jingu Shrine' (804 m across).
notes: Main Shinto shrine of Hokkaido in Maruyama Park.

text.description: Hokkaido Shrine (Hokkaido Jingu) sits inside Maruyama Park in Chūō-ku, and its grounds cover about 180,000 square metres. It was called Sapporo Shrine until 1964 and has stood on this site since 1871. A fire destroyed the building in 1974, and it was restored in 1978. For a phone photo, the best-known frame is the large wooden torii gate at the park-side entrance. Tall trees stand around it, and the approach to the shrine leads away from the gate. The phone icon on the map is in the middle of the shrine grounds, not at the gate itself, so walk over to the park-side entrance. The stone stairway in front of the torii works well if you want a person in the frame, such as a friend walking up the steps. Stand to one side of the central path rather than on it, because that path is reserved for the gods. If you have time, there are two other frames to try. One is Omotesando, the approach lined with cherry trees, which is lovely when they are in bloom. The other is the Reiwa Torii, a stainless-steel gate that reflects its surroundings. The shrine is busy in cherry blossom season and around New Year, and again during the Sapporo Festival from 14 to 16 June, so go early if you want a quiet shot of the gate.
text.geographic_location: Hokkaido Shrine is in Chūō-ku, Sapporo, inside Maruyama Park, and the shrine grounds run alongside the park.
text.directions_text: Check a map or route planner and head for Maruyama Park in Chūō-ku, starting from central Sapporo. Once you are at the park, use your map to find the shrine and its large wooden torii at the park-side entrance. Allow a little extra time to walk in from the park, because the grounds are large. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the torii framed by the trees. If you are close and the top of the gate gets cut off, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), and keep your phone level so the posts do not lean inwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Go to the park-side torii gate (check its position on a map), and stand beside the central path rather than on it. From there the photo shows the large wooden torii framed by tall trees, with the shrine's approach leading away from the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the torii in the middle, with the approach leading the eye into the picture. Include the stone stairway in front of the gate if you want a figure-in-frame shot. For a different view, try Omotesando for the cherry-lined approach, or the Reiwa Torii for the reflective steel gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the torii to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky behind the dark wood is not washed out. Keep your lens clean, as it picks up dust and fingerprints easily outdoors.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds arrive.

text.access_note: The shrine is a place of worship, so be respectful and stay off the central path; check the official site before you go for current opening hours and for any rules on photography, especially if your photos are for commercial use.

name: Sapporo TV Tower
label: Sapporo TV Tower
camera_source: Commons cluster (2 photos), weak. Moved 16 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 40 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/199758828: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sapporo TV Tower' (48 m across).
notes: Tower at the east end of Odori Park with an observation deck.

text.description:
Sapporo TV Tower is a slim tower standing in Odori Park, Sapporo. It was built in 1957 and is 147.2 metres tall. It was designed by Tachū Naitō, the architect also known for planning Tokyo Tower. Digital clocks were added at about 65 metres up in 1961, and they face all four sides. They make a good detail to look for in your photos. An observation deck sits at 90.38 metres, with views over Odori Park, Mount Ōkura and Maruyama.

The tower photographs well because it is tall, simple in shape and set in open parkland, so it stands clear of its surroundings. Many high-rise buildings now surround the park, so it no longer dominates the skyline as it once did. This works in your favour. You can use those buildings as a backdrop and show how the old tower sits among the new ones.

Switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) and tilt the phone upwards to get the whole structure. Expect the sides to lean inwards towards the top. You can use that on purpose for a dramatic shot. For a calmer picture, walk back along the park and use the default lens (1x) or a little zoom. The Sapporo TV Tower is also a good subject for a quick snap of the clocks with the telephoto lens.
text.geographic_location: The tower stands in Odori Park, Sapporo, Hokkaido. Its basement connects to the Aurora Town underground shopping arcade.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Odori Park in Sapporo and look for the tower, which is easy to see. If you are coming from further away, search for Sapporo TV Tower in your maps app. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x), because you are only about 38 m from the base and the tower is 147 m tall. Then try the default lens (1x) or telephoto after stepping back, or for a close-up of the clocks.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 大通公園 (Odori Park) (3-chome section, by the subway exit near the tower). The tower framed from the ground in Odori Park, with the city-name subway exit in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line, so the shot looks tidy. Keep the whole tower in the frame, with some sky above it. For variety, include the trees or lawn of Odori Park in the foreground. Then step back and try a version that shows the nearby high-rise buildings behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the tower to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down a little, so the sky does not wash out. At dusk, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or a wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon are good for softer light and fewer people. Dusk can also work well if the tower is lit.

text.access_note: The tower stands in a public park, but the observation deck needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: At about 38 m from a 147 m tower, a phone's default lens (1x) will not fit the whole tower in the frame, so the ultra-wide lens is needed.
Pointing a phone steeply upwards makes vertical lines lean inwards.
The tower is likely to be lit after dark, so dusk and evening photos may work well.
Early morning and late afternoon usually have softer light and fewer visitors.

name: Sapporo Clock Tower
label: Clock Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sapporo Clock Tower' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/64747104: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sapporo Clock Tower' (44 m across).
notes: Symbol of Sapporo, a wooden 1878 building on Kita 1 Nishi 2.

text.description: Sapporo Clock Tower is a small white-and-green wooden building with a clock tower that now sits among modern office blocks. That contrast is why it photographs so well: the old timber facade, the clock face and the tower make a neat, symmetrical shape against plain glass and concrete behind. It was built in 1878 as the drill hall of the former Sapporo Agricultural College, which is now Hokkaido University. The clock was installed in 1881 by E. Howard & Co. of Boston and still keeps time, with chimes on the hour. It is described as the oldest clock tower in Japan and is widely treated as a symbol of the city. For the classic picture, stand directly in front of the main entrance, where a small photo stage is set up for souvenir shots. From there you get a straight-on view of the whole front. If the grounds are busy, the free terrace of the MN Building across the road gives a slightly higher view of the whole facade. Sapporo City Hall has a viewing corridor looking down on the red roof and clock faces, but it has seasonal and weather limits, so check before going. Allow a few minutes either side of the hour if you would like to hear the chimes while you shoot.
text.geographic_location: The Sapporo Clock Tower stands at North 1 West 2 in Chūō-ku, Sapporo, surrounded by modern office buildings. The MN Building, with its photo terrace, is directly opposite.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so navigate to the address: Sapporo Clock Tower (札幌時計台), North 1 West 2, Chūō-ku. The Sapporo Clock Tower sits right at that address, so once you arrive, step out to the photo stage in front of the main entrance for the best view. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight-on front view. If you cannot fit the whole building in from close up, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. From the Photo Plaza across the road, try telephoto (2x or more) to pick out the clock face and tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step out to the photo stage in the grounds, directly in front of the main entrance. From there you look straight at the wooden facade, clock faces and tower, with the modern office blocks behind. The platform on the right near the intersection is a second option.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the tower up with the centre line so the symmetry works. Hold the phone level and include a little sky above the tower. For a different view, go to the Clock Tower Photo Plaza, a free terrace in the MN Building opposite, which shows the whole front from slightly higher up.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the clock face to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down a little so the white walls and sky keep their detail. If the building is lit after dark, try night mode and rest your elbows on something steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is likely to be calmer around the front of the building. The chimes sound on the hour, so a Live Photo around then adds a little sound and movement.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from public ground and the front is free to stand at, but the museum inside is ticketed and has set opening days, so check the official site before you go, including if you plan to use images commercially.

name: JR Tower
label: JR Tower Observatory
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3041894: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Observation deck on the 38th floor above Sapporo Station.

text.description:
JR Tower is a 38-storey landmark rising above Sapporo Station's South entrance. It stands 173 m high and opened on 6 March 2003. The tower is part of a larger complex that also holds the Stellar Place shopping mall, the Daimaru department store, a cinema, offices and the JR Tower Hotel Nikko Sapporo. Because it sits right on top of the station, it is easy to reach and makes a good first or last photo of a day in the city.

It photographs well because of its height. An upward shot gives a strong vertical line against the sky. Near the base you will not fit the whole thing in unless you use the widest lens, so think about a simple composition: the tower, a slice of sky and perhaps a few passers-by for scale. There is also an observation deck, Tower Three Eight, on the 38th floor. The lift to it starts from the 6th floor and you need a ticket, so check the official site before you go. From up there you can photograph the city rather than the tower itself.

Keep your phone steady against a railing or your own elbows, and wipe the lens before you start, as station areas can be smudgy with fingerprints.
text.geographic_location: JR Tower is in central Sapporo, Hokkaidō, built above the South entrance of JR Sapporo Station. It is joined to the Stellar Place mall and the Daimaru department store.
text.directions_text: Start at JR Sapporo Station, because the tower is built directly above its South entrance. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tower into the frame from close up. Switch to the default lens (1x) if you can step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details, such as the top of the tower against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Tilt the phone upwards from here to catch the full height. If you can, step back a little, so the sides do not lean inwards too much.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line, to keep the sides as straight as possible. Leave some sky above the top. For a second angle, shoot from the 38th-floor observation deck (ticketed) and photograph the city view instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the sky does not wash out. On the observation deck, press the lens close to the window to cut down reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk or early evening, when the sky is darker; check whether the building is lit when you are there. In low light, use night mode and hold the phone still.

text.access_note: The observation deck needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: An upward shot gives a strong vertical line against the sky.
From close to the base you need the ultra-wide lens to fit the whole tower in.
Reflections on the observation deck's windows can be reduced by holding the phone lens close to the glass.
Dusk and early evening are good times to photograph the tower, as the sky is darker.

name: Sapporo Dome
label: Sapporo Dome
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sapporo Dome' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/127094824: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Daiwa House PREMIST DOME' (346 m across).
notes: Futuristic stadium with an observation hall.

text.description: Sapporo Dome is a big, smooth, silver-roofed stadium, and from right outside it the roof fills the frame as a close backdrop. That makes it an easy place for a souvenir photo, whether of the building or of you in front of it. The roof is 245 metres across, so it is hard to miss. The stadium was designed by Hiroshi Hara and finished in March 2001. It hosted three first-round matches of the 2002 FIFA World Cup and was a football venue for the 2020 Summer Olympics. It is now the home ground of Hokkaido Consadole Sapporo. Its name is currently Daiwa House Premist Dome, under a sponsorship deal that runs from 1 August 2024 to 31 July 2028. You may see either name on signs. One unusual feature is that the football pitch is grass and slides in and out of the building when needed. The best photos are taken on the outside, in front of the dome and in the area around it. Walk a little way along the exterior to find a clean angle with few people or cars in the shot. If you want a wider view, Sapporo Hitsujigaoka Observation Hill shows the dome in the distance beyond the grazing sheep, and Okurayama Viewing Point gives a high view of the city with the dome far off. Check the official sites for entry details at both before you go.
text.geographic_location: Sapporo Dome stands in Sapporo, Hokkaido, about a 10-minute walk from Fukuzumi Station.
text.directions_text: Take the Tōhō Line to Fukuzumi Station. From there it is about 10 minutes on foot to the dome. Once you can see the big silver roof, head for the open ground just outside the building, as near the phone icon on the map as you can get. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because from close up the roof is too large for the default lens (1x) to fit. Use the default lens (1x) for photos of people with the dome behind them, or for a tighter view of the roof curve.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the silver roof fills the frame as a close backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the roof's curve up with a grid line so the picture feels balanced. If you are photographing a person, have them stand a few steps in front of you and use the default lens (1x) so the roof does not stretch around them. Keep the phone level, as tilting it makes the building lean. For a different view of the dome, try Sapporo Hitsujigaoka Observation Hill, where you can zoom in (2x-5x, depending on your phone) on the distant dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the roof to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Portrait mode works for photos of people, but keep them a few steps from the building so the edges look clean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a day with some clear sky, when the silver roof stands out well. Morning and late afternoon usually give softer light than midday.

text.access_note: The outside of the dome is where you take the photo, but access around the stadium may be limited on event days, so check the official site before you go.

name: Sapporo Factory
label: Sapporo Factory
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'サッポロファクトリー' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'サッポロファクトリー' (relation/15730185): middle (351 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/15730185: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sapporo Factory' (352 m across).
notes: Red brick former brewery turned shopping complex with a glass atrium.

text.description:
Sapporo Factory is a shopping and leisure complex built into an old brewery, and the red-brick side is where the photos are. The original brewery went up in 1876 for the Kaitakushi, the old Hokkaidō government. It started as a wooden building and was later enlarged in red brick as Sapporo beer became known across Japan. Brewing moved out to Eniwa in 1993, and the buildings were then renovated as the shopping complex you see today.

The best outdoor picture is the courtyard in front of the Renga-kan, the red-brick building on the west side. From there you can frame the old brick facade with its greenery, and the tall black chimney marked 'Sapporo Beer' stands on the square beside the museum. In summer, open beer gardens are often set up in front of the western side of the Renga-kan, which adds colour and life to the scene. In autumn the ivy on the brick wall turns red, and one blogger expected the peak in early November, though this changes from year to year.

If the weather is poor, the glass-roofed Atrium is a good indoor alternative. It has plants along the pathway and fills with daylight, and in winter a tall decorated Christmas tree stands at its centre. Take a few steps back across the courtyard so the whole facade fits, and keep the chimney in the same frame if you can.
text.geographic_location: Sapporo Factory is in Chūō-ku, central Sapporo. It is a short walk from Basusentamae Station, and a little further from Ōdōri Station.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Basusentamae Station on the Tozai line of the Sapporo subway, and it takes about 5 minutes on foot to reach the complex. Ōdōri Station is a little further, and the Tozai line also runs through it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the brick facade, the greenery and the chimney together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view of the brick wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (courtyard in front of the red-brick Renga-kan building, west side of the complex). The old red-brick brewery facade with its greenery and chimney, framed across the open courtyard. From here the old brick facade, its greenery and the chimney are framed across the open courtyard, and the middle of the complex lies to the north-east. Take the Atrium indoors as a second option if you want the glass roof and plants.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the facade with the vertical grid lines so the walls look straight. Include some of the courtyard in the foreground to give a sense of space, and place the chimney on one third of the frame. If you want a different view, the glass-roofed Atrium is a short walk across the courtyard, and works well for a bright indoor shot with plants and benches.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick wall to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright, so the red of the brick stays rich. Use the 2x zoom for close-ups of the ivy or the brickwork rather than pinching in further.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Autumn is the best season, when the ivy on the brick wall turns red. One blogger expected the colour to peak in early November, but it varies by year. Summer also suits the courtyard, as the outdoor beer gardens are often set up in front of the Renga-kan.

text.access_note: The courtyard is an outdoor area within a shopping complex, but shop and event hours vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The courtyard may be busier at weekends and during summer beer-garden events.
Soft, even light on an overcast day or in the morning or late afternoon tends to suit red brick well.
Lowering the exposure slider can help keep brick colours rich when the sky is bright.

name: Mount Moiwa
label: Mount Moiwa
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3290130027: the OpenStreetMap point 'Mount Moiwa'.
notes: Famous night view of Sapporo from the summit observation deck.

text.description:
Mount Moiwa is a mountain to the south-west of the centre of Sapporo, about 5 km away and 6 km from Sapporo Station. It is a popular outing for both local people and visitors. A ropeway and a motorway pass through the mountain, there is an observatory, and in winter it doubles as a ski resort. That mix of uses is why it makes a good photo stop: you can come for a daytime view, a dusk shot or a snowy scene, depending on the season.

If there is a clear view of the city from where you stand, it can give you a big, layered picture of Sapporo. Start with the wide view, then look for smaller scenes inside it, such as a stretch of streets, a line of trees or the edge of the hills. If you use the observatory, stand a little back from the glass so reflections don't spoil the shot. The weather changes the picture a lot. Clear air gives a long, crisp view, while low cloud or haze gives a softer, moodier one.

In winter, wrap up warm and keep your phone in an inside pocket between shots, because cold drains the battery quickly. Ropeway and observatory access can change with the season, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Mount Moiwa lies in the south-west of Sapporo, Hokkaido, about 5 km from the city centre and 6 km from Sapporo Station.
text.directions_text: Mount Moiwa lies about 6 km south-west of Sapporo Station. A ropeway and a motorway both pass through the mountain, so check the official site for current access before you visit. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main view over the city. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to include more sky or a wide sweep of the hills. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as a patch of streets or a line of buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face towards the city and keep any railings, signs or other people out of the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the top or bottom line, depending on whether the sky or the city is more interesting. Include a little foreground, such as trees or a rail, to give the picture depth. Try one wide shot, then a closer zoomed shot of one part of the view. A panorama can work well for a sweeping view, so move slowly and keep the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the city to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so bright sky doesn't wash out. At dusk, use night mode and hold your phone steady against a rail or your own body. If you shoot through glass, press the lens close to it to cut reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk usually gives the best mix of soft light and city lights. Clear days give the longest views.

text.access_note: Access to the ropeway, observatory and any viewing areas may be ticketed or seasonal, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: If there is a clear view of the city from where you stand, it can give a wide, layered picture of Sapporo.
Dusk and late afternoon usually give soft light and visible city lights.
Reflections in observatory windows can spoil photos, and pressing the phone against the glass reduces them.
Cold winter weather drains phone batteries quickly.
Ropeway and observatory access may be ticketed or vary by season.
Cloud or haze can change the look of the view.

name: Former Hokkaido Government Office
label: Red Brick Office
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Former Hokkaido Government Office' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/36331476: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Former Hokkaido Government Office Building' (79 m across).
notes: The historic Red Brick building from 1888.

text.description:
The former Hokkaido Government Office is a red-brick building whose pond view guides call the classic postcard shot. It was inaugurated in 1888, and the walls hold around 2.5 million bricks made in what are now Toyohira and Shiroishi wards. The octagonal dome on top was taken off in 1896, then put back in 1968 for the prefecture's 100th anniversary. The building became a National Important Cultural Property the following year. It is about 61 metres wide and 33 metres high to the top of the tower.

It photographs well because the whole front is clean and symmetrical, and there is a pond and flower garden in front. From the far side of the water you can fit the full facade in one frame with its reflection below. A phone copes well with this: the default lens (1x) takes in the building and the water together without much fuss. The red brick also stands out against green leaves or snow, so the colour does much of the work.

If you want a different view, the avenue leading to the building gives a long perspective with trees on both sides, and an upper-floor viewpoint at Akarenga Terrace looks down over it. Renovation works have been reported at the building, so scaffolding or screens may cover part of the facade or garden. Check current conditions before you go.
text.geographic_location: In central Sapporo, close to the Archives of Hokkaido annex at West 5. The building sits at the end of a tree-lined approach avenue, with its flower garden and pond in front.
text.directions_text: Navigate to the Former Hokkaido Government Office (the red-brick building) by name. The phone icon on the map marks the building itself. Once there, walk into the front garden and head for the pond, then stand on the far side of the water facing the building. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the pond to get the whole facade and its reflection. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you have to stand close. Use 2x or more on the dome and tower for a tighter shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Walk out to the front garden on the Former Hokkaido Government Office grounds and stand on the far side of the pond, facing the building. From there you see the full red-brick facade with the pond in the foreground, so the building reflects in the water. Adjust on site until the reflection sits well.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water's edge on the lower third line, with the building centred above it. This keeps the reflection and the symmetry tidy. Hold the phone level so the walls stay straight. For a different view, try the long tree-lined avenue at Kita 3-jo Plaza (Akapla), where the trees frame the building in perspective.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the red brick keeps its colour and the sky does not wash out. Wait for a moment when the water is still before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a calm day, as wind ripples the pond and breaks up the reflection. Visit when the garden is in flower or when leaves or snow set off the red brick.

text.access_note: The garden is in front of the building and the building has been described as free to enter, but renovation works have been reported, so check the official site before you go.

name: Okurayama Ski Jump Stadium
label: Okurayama Ski Jump
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '大倉山ジャンプ競技場' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '大倉山ジャンプ競技場' (way/267873727): middle (559 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/267873727: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Okurayama Ski Jump Stadium' (559 m across).
notes: Olympic ski jump hill with a view over the city.

text.description: Okurayama is Sapporo's big ski jump, set on the eastern slope of Mt. Okura in the Miyanomori area. It photographs well because the slope is so steep and the structure so tall. From the bottom you look straight up the in-run and the approach, and nothing else on the hill shows the scale as clearly. The jump was built in 1931 by Kishichiro Okura and given to the city. It was rebuilt for the 1972 Winter Olympics, when it hosted the 90 metre class event. Today it is a large hill, 133 metres from the top start to the foot of the slope, and its steepest stretches are around 35 to 37 degrees. Include a few people or the grounds at the bottom so the height reads properly. To get here you ride a moving staircase up from the car park. The Crystal House (shop and restaurant) is near the entrance and the Winter Sports Museum is on the other side. If you want the opposite view, the observation platform at the top looks down the runway to the city. The lift to it needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the Miyanomori area of Chūō-ku, Sapporo, on the eastern slope of Mt. Okura, on the western side of the city centre.
text.directions_text: A JR Bus runs from Maruyama Bus Terminal (Maruyama-Kōen Station, Tōzai Line) to the Okurayama Kyogijo Iriguchi bus stop in about 12 minutes. From there it is about 10 minutes on foot to the stadium. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) at the base of the jump to fit the whole steep structure in. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of the in-run. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the top of the in-run and the take-off ramp.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (base of the jump, looking up at the in-run and the steep approach). The full steep jump structure rising above you, which shows its scale most clearly. From here you look up the in-run and the steep approach, and the whole structure rises above you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright (portrait) and tilt it up so the slope runs from the bottom corner towards the top of the frame. Turn on gridlines and keep the sides of the slope straight so the jump doesn't lean. A person or two at the bottom gives a sense of scale. For a different view, the observation platform at the top shows the runway and Sapporo city, but it needs a lift ticket.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the slope to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out the structure. Try a Live Photo if people are on the grounds, to catch some movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in daylight, when the jump is open and the structure is clear against the sky. Mornings may suit the east-facing slope best.

text.access_note: The grounds are open to visitors on foot, but the jump and lift may close on competition or practice days, during lift maintenance and in bad weather, and the lift to the top needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The slope faces east, so it may catch morning light (inferred from it being on the eastern slope of Mt. Okura).
From the base of the jump, the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens is likely needed to fit the whole structure in.
The grounds are open to visitors on foot (from the researched viewpoint notes; hours and closures should be checked).

name: Hokkaido University poplar avenue
label: Poplar Avenue
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '北大ポプラ並木' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: '北12条西10' (pois).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q21654580: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Tree-lined avenue on the Hokkaido University campus.

text.description: This is the long, straight line of tall poplars on the Hokkaido University campus, and it is one of the best-known sights in Sapporo. The tree trunks rise in neat rows and the leafy canopy closes overhead, so the view draws the eye down the avenue. It looks fresh and green in summer and golden in autumn. The avenue is a well-known symbol of the university, and Japan's national tourism website for visitors lists it among Sapporo's three most famous attractions. The first poplars came from America in the early 1900s, and the avenue took shape in 1912 as a windbreak for the college farm. Typhoons have hit it hard. In 2004 only 32 of roughly 50 trees were left, and new saplings were planted to fill the gaps. Walking among the trees is often not allowed, so respect any fences or signs. The view from the path is the classic postcard one: rows of trunks running away from you under the leaves. Keep the phone level so the trunks stay straight, and let the rows lead the eye.
text.geographic_location: In the Hokkaido University campus in Kita-ku, Sapporo. The avenue runs from behind the Psychology Department towards the first of the university's farms.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed close to this spot, so head for the Hokkaido University campus in Kita-ku, Sapporo. Car access on the campus is restricted, so arrive on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the natural view down the rows. Try 2x or more to pack the trunks closer together, or the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the canopy.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (from the path alongside the avenue, not inside the rows). The tall, straight poplar rows receding along the avenue, framed by the trees' green or autumn-yellow canopy. On the path alongside the avenue, not inside the rows. From here you can see the tall, straight poplar rows receding along the avenue under their green or autumn-yellow canopy.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the avenue with the centre of the frame so the rows meet at one point in the distance. Keep the phone upright and level. If the main avenue is fenced off, shoot from behind the fence and don't step past it. For a quieter alternative, the newer Heisei poplar avenue (平成ポプラ並木) is a straight row with a clear one-point perspective, about 500 m to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the trees to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky doesn't wash out and the leaves keep their colour. Use portrait mode if you want to include a person, but keep them on the path.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Summer for fresh green leaves and autumn for yellow. Visit early in the day if you want a quieter path.

text.access_note: Access among the trees is often restricted, so please check the official site before you go and photograph from the adjacent path.

name: Hokkaido University Botanic Garden
label: Botanic Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'めがね橋' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: '北3条西9' (pois); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/102474363: large area 'Botanical Garden of Hokkaido University' (607 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Historic garden with greenhouses and a museum near the centre.

text.description: Hokkaido University Botanic Garden is a calm green pocket of Sapporo, and the red-brick arch bridge over its pond is the most photogenic corner. Brick, water, water plants and old trees sit close together, so a single phone frame can hold all of them. The garden opened in 1886 as part of the former Sapporo Agricultural College. It is now the second oldest botanic garden in Japan. It covers 13.3 hectares and holds a small patch of the forest that once covered the Ishikari Plain, plus more than 4,000 plant species. There is also a lilac said to be the oldest in Sapporo. The white Natural History Museum building dates from 1884 and is worth a frame of its own if you have time. For the bridge shot, stand on the bridge and face north. Let the arch and its reflection fill the lower third of the frame, with the trees behind. If you want a second picture, the North Lawn (北ローン), a wide open lawn, has large old trees around its edges and gives a clean, airy view. The museum (博物館本館) photographs well from the front. If other visitors are in frame, wait a moment for a clear gap rather than rushing. The garden charges admission, and the outdoor grounds may be closed for the winter months, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The garden is in Chūō-ku, Sapporo, and is operated by Hokkaido University. The brick bridge is over the pond inside the garden.
text.directions_text: No public-transport stop is listed for this spot, so check a map app or the official site for the best way to reach the garden (北海道大学植物園). Inside, follow the paths to the pond and the red-brick arch bridge. The bridge is only a short stroll from the middle of the garden. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the bridge and pond. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the bridge feels cramped, or to 2x-3x telephoto for a tighter shot of the arch and the water plants.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on めがね橋 (brick arch bridge over the pond; stand on the bridge and face north). The red-brick arch bridge framed by the pond and the surrounding trees, with the water plants in view. Keep facing north for the bridge view. From here you see the red-brick arch bridge framed by the pond and the surrounding trees, with the water plants in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the bridge's arch and its reflection along the lower third, with the trees filling the rest. Keep the phone level so the bridge rail does not slope. For a second viewpoint, try the wide open lawn (北ローン) with its old trees around the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright part of the sky or water to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the brick stays rich and the sky is not washed out. A Live Photo can catch ripples or a passing bird.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The outdoor grounds are open in the warmer months, so plan for late spring to autumn when the trees are in leaf. Gentle morning or late-afternoon light, or a soft overcast day, usually flatters brick and water.

text.access_note: The garden is a ticketed site, and the outdoor grounds may be closed from early November to late April, so check the official site before you go.
